journey:rouault-miserere.l: Impressions in many collections, including the Museum of Modern Art (New York) and the Haggerty Museum of Art, Marquette University (Milwaukee)
journey:rouault-miserere.m: Series of 58 prints: etching, aquatint and drypoint over photogravure
journey:rouault-miserere.noimg: © ADAGP, Paris (Georges Rouault estate). View impressions in the collections of the Museum of Modern Art, New York, and other museums.

x.summary: Rouault's Miserere, a cycle of 58 large prints, is a meditation on human suffering, conceived before 1914 and largely drawn during the First World War. Again and again the cycle returns to the face of the suffering Christ, crowned with thorns or hanging on the cross, among images of war, poverty and grief. Its heavy black lines, often linked to Rouault's early training as a stained-glass apprentice, give the plates the solemn weight of a church window.
facts: The title comes from Psalm 51, 'Miserere mei, Deus' ('Have mercy on me, O God').

Starting from images of his own drawings transferred to copper, Rouault worked and reworked each plate; in his 1948 preface he wrote that he sometimes went through twelve or fifteen successive states.

The series was undertaken for the dealer Ambroise Vollard, and the printing was finished in 1927; but after Vollard's death in 1939, the Second World War and a lawsuit against Vollard's heirs, the cycle was published only in 1948.
